title: What is known about 1RB1RD_1LC0RD_0LE1RD_1RA0RB_---1LF_1RA0LF
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RD_1LC0RD_0LE1RD_1RA0RB_---1LF_1RA0LF.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The machine keeps a long block of identical words and, right of it, a row of unary counters. For long stretches each period of 160 new cells does the same thing (block +14 words, first counter −6, the next two +4 each); when the first counter runs out the row is reorganised in a way that depends on the counters' residues, as in a Collatz-type map.

An exact accelerated simulator followed it through 100,000 such regimes without a halt: the machine does not halt in its first 9.53·10<sup>2780</sup> steps (trusted computation, validated against a plain simulator and against a second implementation). Whether it ever halts is not known.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: The long crossings
claims.text: For every n and every tape around: B, with 01111 behind it, turns (01010000000)<sup>n+1</sup> into (01111111111)<sup>n+1</sup> in 53 steps a word; F, on the first of twelve 0s, turns (01111111111)<sup>n</sup> on its left into (10100000000)<sup>n</sup> on its right in 19 steps a word; and F on the first of four 0s turns (011)<sup>n</sup> into (101)<sup>n</sup> in 11 steps a word.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: Where it can halt
claims.text: The halting transition E0 is reached only through B1 → 0RD, D1 → 0RB, B0 → 1LC, C0 → 0LE: the machine halts exactly when B reads a 1 followed by 1 0 (read off the table).

claims.title: The linear regime
claims.text: Sampled every 160 new cells at the left end: the bulk gains 14 words, the first counter loses 6, the next two gain 4 each, until the first counter runs out and the list is reorganised.

claims.title: Two exact accelerated simulators
claims.text: accsim.c crosses runs of words by shift rules it establishes at run time (one word simulated, same state and same cells behind it at the next word); accbig.c adds jumps over linear regimes (14 equal samples, counts and step counts extrapolated exactly) and big integers. Same step counts as a plain simulator at 216 events, as each other at 230 events (2.3·1017 steps, 172 jumps), and as a second implementation with capped jumps at 3.66·1018 events (2.65·1036 steps).

claims.title: No halt in the first 9.53·10<sup>2780</sup> steps
claims.text: accbig passes 100,000 linear regimes without a halt and stops at event 6.94·101390 after 9.53·102780 steps (exact numbers of 1,391 and 2,781 digits in c/accbig_run.txt). The jumps over regimes rest on the argument in the program's header and on the validations, not on a machine-checked proof.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The reorganisations of the counter list are Collatz-like; an exact map for them (finite, by residues and separators) is the next step, towards an invariant or towards a halting case.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RC_1RC1RA_1LD0RA_0LE1RA_---1LF_1RB0LF up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has been followed, by an exact shortcut simulation, for more than 10<sup>2780</sup> steps without stopping. It behaves like a row of counters pouring into each other, and nobody can predict where that leads.

facts.text: No halt (exact accelerated simulation through 100,000 regimes).
The long sweeps through the block and the counters, proved for every length.
What one period does to the first three counters, until the first runs out.

sections.heading: A block of words and a row of counters
html: Most of the tape is one 11-cell word repeated thousands, then millions of times (the bulk). Right of it sits a short row of counters: runs of the word 101, separated by a few other cells. The head shuttles between the left end of the tape and the counters, sweeping through the bulk on the way; these long sweeps are proved in Lean for a bulk of any length.
For long stretches every period does the same thing: the bulk grows by 14 words, the first counter loses 6 and the next two gain 4 each. So the first counter is slowly poured into its two neighbours.

sections.heading: When a counter runs dry
html: When the first counter is empty, the machine rearranges the front of the row: the separators change and the next counter becomes the first. What exactly comes out depends on how much was left over at that moment (the counter's remainder when divided by 6, and so on down the row). The deep counters are fed only at these moments, by amounts that depend on remainders of the counters above them.

That is the same kind of rule as in the Collatz problem (“halve it if even, otherwise triple it and add one”): easy to follow step by step, very hard to predict in the long run. The machine stops only if, at some rearrangement, a counter boundary comes up out of phase, so that the head reads 1 1 0 where it always read 1 0 1 before.

sections.heading: More than 10<sup>2780</sup> steps, exactly
html: Each stretch between two rearrangements is longer than the one before, so the machine cannot be followed step by step for long. But a stretch is completely regular, and its length and its effect can be computed exactly in one go. A simulator that crosses repeated words in one move and whole stretches in one move, with exact big-number arithmetic, followed the machine through 100,000 rearrangement stretches. It did not halt: the first 9.53·102780 steps (a number with 2,781 digits) contain no halt.

The simulator was checked against a plain step-by-step simulator as far as that can go, and against a second, differently built version further out. It is a trusted computation, not a proof: and it cannot say what happens later.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

family: bouncer feeding a cascade of unary counters (Collatz-like)
summary: A bulk of 11-cell words grows at the left (14 words per 160 new cells) and feeds a cascade of unary counters (101)^c at the right: the first counter drains into the next two (-6, +4, +4) and the list is reorganised, Collatz-like, when it runs out. Exact accelerated simulation (shift rules found at run time, jumps over the linear regimes, big integers) through 100,000 regimes: no halt in the first 9.53·10^2780 steps.
